newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists rap centre-right manifesto plans.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists rap centre-right manifesto plans.

text.p: French Socialists dismissed the ruling centre-right's new policy plans as more of the same failed medicine on Monday as two surveys showed the coalition winning next month's election, possibly by a narrow margin.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Sunday announced a 40-day flurry of legislation if his coalition wins re-election in the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election, promising spending caps to help qualify for a single European currency as well as tax cuts.

He also pledged to help reduce record unemployment by cutting payroll charges on low wages, reduce the number of government ministries to 15, make working hours more flexible and pursue decentralisation.
"The Right wants to enter the 21st century by reinstating the labour relations of the 19th century," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin told a rally in Blois south-west of Paris.

"There is no change, this is the same policy. But as he is aware it is not very attractive. Juppe has stolen from the Socialist programme, especially on a cut in working hours," said party spokesman Francois Hollande.
He said most of Juppe's policies had already been submitted to the National Assembly and accused the government of secretly planning a new round of cuts to qualify for the euro.

Jospin said earlier he would seek on Tuesday an election pact with the Communists, who oppose a planned single European currency favoured by the Socialists, and that the next government may include Communist ministers.

Asked whether he planned to take Communists into government if the Socialists won, Jospin told Europe 1 radio: "The only problem is that of government cohesion. If there were to be a left-wing government, it could only be formed if there was only one clear political stance, including on Europe."
Hollande said the declaration would not seek to harmonise policies where the parties were at odds, as over the euro.

The Socialists are in favour of the euro although they have set conditions and refused further austerity steps to reach the strict budget deficit criterion for European monetary union. The Communists oppose a single currency and want a referendum on the issue.

"After trying to hide their Communist ally from public opinion, in refusing for example to take part in a (four-way) televised debate suggested by Mr Juppe, the Socialists are now studying the participation of Communist ministers," Juppe's Gaullist RPR said in a statement.
"All this lacks coherence and illustrates the disarray in which the Socialist Party is sinking," it said.
The newspaper Le Monde said the RPR and its centrist allies in the UDF would unveil a manifesto on Tuesday fleshing out the policies outlined by Juppe.
It said the manifesto's stated aim is to "succeed in achieving the euro on January 1, 1999" and also to institute "a true social Europe which would avoid unfair competition among European countries."
The text notes the coalition's determination "to stabilise public spending so that it does not progress faster than inflation" but does not elaborate, the newspaper said.
A poll out on Monday showed the centre-right heading for a narrow majority but found more than one-third of voters could change their minds.

The BVA poll for France 2 television said that the ruling coalition would win 296 of the 555 seats in metropolitan France, the Socialists 238, the Communists 18, the ecologists two and the far-right National Front one.

A separate Louis Harris poll for the Politique Opinion magazine credited the centre-right coalition with 40 percent of voting intentions and the leftist bloc with 38 percent. Eighteen percent expressed no opinion.
"The situation has never been so tight...There is a very great instability and uncertainty about voters' behaviour in the second round," said Pierre Giacometti of the IPSOS polling institute.
